extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for handling exposition, backstory, flashbacks, narration, and audience engagement in screenplays and dramatic storytelling; includes how to create curiosity/concern, Turning Points, and manage revelations. Focuses on craft techniques to dramatize information and sustain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition means facts—the information about setting, biography, and characterization that the audience needs to know to follow and comprehend the events of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-done exposition should be invisible; the audience absorbs what it needs effortlessly. Skill in exposition tells us the writer knows the craft. Examples and anti-patterns (table-dusting, forced dialogue) illustrate poor exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Never force words into a character's mouth to tell the audience about world, history, or person. Instead, dramatize exposition—show honest, natural scenes where characters talk and behave truthfully while indirectly passing along necessary facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let camera or narration simply 'tell' a chain of facts (e.g., panning photographs). 'Show, don't tell' also means characters and camera must behave truthfully; avoid turning film into a home movie or illustrated audio book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatized exposition primary/secondary purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatized exposition serves two ends: its primary purpose is to further the immediate conflict; its secondary purpose is to convey information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novices often reverse the order by putting expositional duty ahead of dramatic necessity. Always ensure exposition furthers dramatic action rather than halting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert exposition to ammunition
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert exposition to ammunition: characters use their knowledge as weapons in their struggle to get what they want so exposition becomes part of conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: replace unmotivated telling with lines that attack, bait, or provoke—audience infers facts (e.g., 'twenty years' learned via reaction rather than spoken summary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unmotivated confessions ('California scenes')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write scenes where strangers exchange intimate life secrets for no believable dramatic motivation—these are forced and false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such ready-made confessions (the 'California scene') feel like prepared anecdotes; they reveal nothing real because whatever is said hides what cannot be said. Confessions must be plausibly motivated by stakes and pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never include what audience can assume
rubrics_metrics.description: Never include anything the audience can reasonably and easily assume has happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only pass on exposition that, if missing, would cause confusion. Withhold information except what is absolutely necessary for comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace exposition progressively
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition must have a progressive pattern: least important facts first, more important facts later, critical facts last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical pieces are secrets or painful truths. Pace disclosure so revelations escalate toward climaxes; parsing exposition throughout the story maintains interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save the best for last (temporal principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obey the temporal art principle: Save the best for last—revealing too much too soon lets the audience see climaxes coming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal only what the audience absolutely needs and wants to know; create dramatic pressure so the final revelations have maximal impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create desire to know (arouse curiosity)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a piece of exposition must be known at a point, create the desire to know by arousing curiosity—pose 'Why?' questions in the audience's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'Why is this character behaving this way?' to make the audience hungry for information so complicated dramatized facts pass smoothly into understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin in medias res and use a Spine
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin the story in medias res—close in time to the climactic event—so the protagonist's biography before the Inciting Incident is lengthened and story duration compressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most stories follow a Spine (single deep desire) over months/weeks/hours. Lifelong Spines are rare and require enormous power to sustain a unified story over decades; otherwise narratives become episodic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose protagonists with something to lose (stakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell stories about people who have something to lose—family, careers, ideals, reputations—as those stakes generate jeopardy and conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High stakes provide ammunition for dramatized exposition; low-stakes lives (e.g., a homeless alcoholic with nothing to lose) make it hard to create an active Spine and lead to static portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'table-dusting' expository devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid scenes where expository dialogue is used as convenient background (e.g., servants reciting household history while dusting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This nineteenth-century playwright trick is still seen today and marks amateur writing; always motivate exposition within character goals or conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning Points: only action or revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes can be turned only on action or on revelation—these are the two means to create Turning Points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example action turn: a slap and breakup. Example revelation turn: confessing an affair. Most scenes need a mix, but some major turns are best achieved via revelation from Backstory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Backstory for powerful revelations
rubrics_metrics.description: Backstory (previous significant events) provides revelations that, if saved for critical moments, create explosive Turning Points and open gaps between expectation and result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve backstory revelations for major Turning Points and act climaxes to maximize impact (examples: CHINATOWN and THE EMPIRE STRIKES BACK).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flashbacks are exposition and must be dramatized
rubrics_metrics.description: The flashback is a form of exposition and should be handled like other exposition—dramatize it by interpolating a minidrama with its own Inciting Incident, progression, and Turning Point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-done flashbacks can accelerate pace; badly done ones bore. Use flashbacks to answer an audience-created need for information, not as gratuitous background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay flashbacks until audience needs them
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not bring in a flashback until you have created in the audience the need and desire to know the past events being shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: CASABLANCA only flashes back to Paris when the audience is burning with curiosity after the Act One Climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Dream Sequences skeptically
rubrics_metrics.description: Dream sequences are exposition 'in a ball gown' and usually feeble; the earlier principles of dramatization apply doubly to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most dream sequences disguise information in clichés; use only when they genuinely serve dramatized revelation (exception examples like WILD STRAWBERRIES).

rubrics_metrics.name: Montage caution
rubrics_metrics.description: In American use, a montage is a series of rapidly cut images used to condense or expand time and convey information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montages are often a lazy attempt to substitute decorative photography and editing for dramatization and should generally be avoided except in exceptional, well-motivated cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice-over narration test and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice-over narration is another way to divulge exposition; test it by asking, 'If I stripped the voice-over out, would the story still be well told?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep narration only if it adds counterpoint or elements that cannot be conveyed otherwise. Apply 'less is more'; remove anything that can be cut. Avoid turning cinema into 'books-on-tape' with explanatory voice-over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the audience's intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Show, don't tell' also means respect the intelligence and sensitivity of your audience; invite them to watch, think, feel, and draw conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid patronizing explanations and overuse of narration that eliminates curiosity and narrative drive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem of Interest: capture both curiosity and concern
rubrics_metrics.description: To hold audience interest, a story must attract both sides of human nature—intellect (curiosity) and emotion (concern).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curiosity asks questions and seeks answers (each Turning Point hooks curiosity). Concern is an emotional focus on positive values (justice, survival, love) toward which empathy flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curiosity (intellectual engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiosity is the intellectual need to answer questions and close open patterns; story exploits this by posing questions and opening situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each Turning Point should hook curiosity—'What's going to happen next?'—and withhold answers until climaxes to keep the audience engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern and the Center of Good (emotional engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern is the emotional need for positive values. The audience searches for a Center of Good—some positive focus for empathy—and it must be located at least in the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Center of Good need not mean 'nice'; it's a relative positive against a negative environment. Writers manage moral balance around the protagonist to draw empathy (examples: THE GODFATHER, WHITE HEAT, SILENCE OF THE LAMBS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery vs Suspense vs Dramatic Irony (audience/character knowledge relationships)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three ways to connect audience to story based on information balance: Mystery (audience knows less than characters), Suspense (audience and characters know the same), Dramatic Irony (audience knows more than characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mystery: use curiosity, red herrings, Closed vs Open Mystery conventions. Suspense: combine curiosity and concern, outcome uncertain—this is the dominant mode. Dramatic Irony: emphasizes concern/dread and deeper focus on motivations; often opens with ending. These modes can be mixed within a Suspense design to varying effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed vs Open Mystery conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed Mystery (Agatha Christie): murder in Backstory, multiple suspects, red herrings; Open Mystery (Columbo): audience sees the murder, story becomes 'How will he catch him?' with emphasis on a fatal flaw in an otherwise perfect crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers must develop multiple suspects for Closed Mysteries and craft elaborate crimes with a logical fatal flaw for Open Mysteries. Subgenre conventions determine audience expectations and should be respected or intentionally subverted.
